chapter_title: Advanced Mecanim: Blend Trees and Layers

screens.title: Advanced Mecanim: Blend Trees and Layers
screens.subtitle: Build smooth locomotion with Blend Trees and isolate gestures with Animation Layers and Avatar Masks

narration.text: In this chapter you will learn two complementary Mecanim systems that let characters move and act at the same time. First, Blend Trees let you merge multiple clips into a single responsive motion driven by parameters like Speed, so transitions between idle, walk, and run become smooth and natural. Second, Animation Layers let you play separate state machines concurrently, and Avatar Masks let you limit a layer to specific body parts so a wave or punch only affects the upper body while locomotion continues. You will see concrete steps for creating a 1D Blend Tree, assigning thresholds, and linking a float parameter. You'll also build an UpperBody layer, create an Avatar Mask that selects spine and arms, and toggle that layer's weight from a simple C# script. Throughout, we'll point out common mistakes — like mismatched thresholds or masks that include unintended bones — and show small checks to avoid them. By the end you'll understand both the authoring workflow in the Animator and how to control these features at runtime.

keyIdea.text: Blend Trees create smooth parameter-driven blends; Animation Layers plus Avatar Masks allow concurrent, isolated animations on different body parts.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you should be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: In this block of objectives we set clear, verifiable outcomes. First, you'll understand why Blend Trees are used to create smooth blends between multiple clips rather than switching states. This matters because parameter-driven blending reduces visual pops and produces natural movement. Second, you'll be able to implement both 1D and 2D Blend Trees, choosing parameters and thresholds that match your animation clips. An example outcome is building a Speed-driven 1D Blend Tree that moves a character from idle to run fluidly. Third, you'll learn to use Animation Layers to run separate state machines at the same time; this is useful for combining locomotion with upper-body gestures. Fourth, you'll configure Avatar Masks so a layer only affects the intended bones; for instance, limiting a wave to the spine and arms while leaving the legs to a locomotion blend. Each objective includes a small mnemonic and a verified competency milestone to mark progress.

screens.title: What is a Blend Tree?
screens.subtitle: A single Animator state that mixes multiple clips based on parameters

narration.text: A Blend Tree is a special Animator state that blends several animation clips together based on one or more parameters. Instead of creating separate states with transitions for every small speed change, you place your clips inside a Blend Tree and map them to numeric thresholds. As the driving parameter changes, the Animator interpolates between clips so motion shifts smoothly. For example, with a Speed parameter a 1D Blend Tree can map Idle to threshold 0, Walk to threshold 2, and Run to threshold 5. When Speed moves between 2 and 5 the system mixes Walk and Run so you never see a sudden cut. One common misconception is that Blend Trees magically fix poor animation loops. They don't: the clips themselves must loop cleanly and align at their boundaries. Blend Trees handle mixing, not correcting mismatched poses. In practice, use Blend Trees for locomotion, direction-driven stances, and layered facial blends. Key checks include setting thresholds that reflect actual parameter ranges and previewing the blend to verify crossfades. Takeaway: Blend Trees simplify state machines by replacing many discrete states with a parameter-driven blend that produces fluid motion.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Blend Trees let you blend multiple clips by parameter values to create smooth, continuous animation states.

content.html:
Core Concept
Blend Tree — definition

A parameter-driven state that mixes multiple animation clips together so transitions are continuous rather than discrete.

Why this matters
  • Reduces state explosion in the Animator by consolidating related motions.
  • Creates smoother visual transitions controlled by runtime parameters.
  • Makes tuning locomotion faster because thresholds can be previewed and adjusted.
Common misconception
Blend Trees do not fix poorly looped clips. Ensure clips loop cleanly for good blends.

Key Takeaway

Use Blend Trees when several clips represent the same conceptual state and should be mixed by a parameter.

screens.title: Creating a 1D Blend Tree
screens.subtitle: Step-by-step setup for locomotion driven by a Speed float

narration.text: Let's walk through creating a 1D Blend Tree for locomotion. Start by opening the Animator window and right-clicking to create a new state: Create State → From New Blend Tree. Name the state Locomotion and double-click it to open the Blend Tree editor. In the Parameters tab add a float parameter called Speed and select it as the blend parameter. Then add motion fields: add the Idle clip with Threshold 0, the Walk clip with Threshold 2, and the Run clip with Threshold 5. After placing clips, preview the blend by scrubbing the Speed value in the editor and check that the visual mix looks natural. Next, create transitions from your default Idle state to Locomotion using Speed > 0.1 and back with Speed <= 0.1, removing Has Exit Time and setting a small Transition Duration like 0.2. A practical pitfall is picking thresholds that the runtime Speed never reaches; always align thresholds with your input mapping and expected top speed. Finally, verify that clips intended to loop have Loop Time enabled in their import settings so the blend remains seamless when the character is moving continuously.

keyIdea.title: Step-by-step
keyIdea.text: Create Locomotion as a 1D Blend Tree, set Speed thresholds, add motion fields, preview and tie transitions to parameter conditions.

content.html:
Process Flow
Create 1D Blend Tree
  1. 1. Right-click in Animator → Create State → From New Blend Tree. Name it Locomotion.
  2. 2. Add a float parameter named Speed and select it as the Blend Tree parameter.
  3. 3. Add motion fields: Idle (0), Walk (2), Run (5) and set Thresholds accordingly.
  4. 4. Create transitions: Idle → Locomotion when Speed > 0.1 and back when Speed <= 0.1. Uncheck Has Exit Time.
  5. 5. Preview blend by scrubbing Speed and adjust thresholds to match runtime input ranges.
Example thresholds
0
Idle
2
Walk
5
Run
Example check
If Run never appears in playtest, lower its threshold or raise the input mapping so Speed reaches that value.
Key Takeaway

Thresholds must reflect the actual range of your runtime parameter, and clips should loop if intended for continuous motion.

screens.title: 1D vs 2D Blend Trees
screens.subtitle: Choosing the right blend type for locomotion and directional movement

narration.text: Blend Trees come in several flavors. A 1D Blend blends clips along a single parameter axis such as Speed, ideal for idle, walk, and run cycles. A 2D Blend takes two parameters, often InputX and InputY, and is useful for directional movement where you need forward, backward, and strafing animations. There are variations like Freeform and Simple Directional that assume symmetry or allow arbitrary placement. Use 1D when motion is primarily speed-scaled along one axis; use 2D when you need direction-aware transitions, such as moving diagonally. A frequent mistake is using a 2D blend when a 1D blend suffices, which increases authoring cost without benefit. Conversely, using 1D for directional movement can produce odd blends if clips represent significantly different directions. When authoring 2D blends, position clips on the parameter plane according to their directional influence and preview combinations at corner and diagonal positions. Remember also that Direct Blends exist when you want to control each clip weight explicitly with parameters rather than thresholds, but they are more manual. Choose the type that matches the conceptual control you need. 1D vs 2D Blend Trees means use 1d for single-parameter blends like speed; use 2d for direction-based blends using two parameters for richer directional control.. In practical terms, choosing the right blend type for locomotion and directional movement. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Comparison
keyIdea.text: Use 1D for single-parameter blends like Speed; use 2D for direction-based blends using two parameters for richer directional control.

content.html:
Comparison
1D Blend

Best when a single numeric factor drives motion. Example: Speed controls Idle → Walk → Run.

  • Pros: Simple to author, predictable blending.
  • Cons: Not suitable for directional nuance.
2D Blend

Use when two parameters control motion, typically horizontal and vertical input for strafing and diagonal motion.

  • Pros: Rich directional control, smoother diagonal blends.
  • Cons: More clips to author and position.
Authoring tip
Map clips on the parameter plane to match their actual directional influence. Preview corner cases: full forward, full right, and diagonals to ensure natural blends.

screens.title: Drive a Blend Tree from script
screens.subtitle: Understanding the provided PlayerMovementAnimator example

narration.text: The supplied C# snippet shows a simple pattern for driving a float parameter in the Animator. The script accumulates a currentSpeed value from input and clamps it between 0 and 5, which matches the thresholds used in the Blend Tree example. Each frame the script calls SetFloat with the Speed parameter to update the Animator. When implementing this pattern, ensure the Speed parameter name matches exactly what you selected in the Animator. Also note two important runtime considerations: first, how you compute currentSpeed must reflect your input mapping and movement logic so thresholds are reachable; second, decide whether root motion is driving actual transform movement or if a separate character controller is used. A common misconception is that large instantaneous speed changes will automatically look good in the Blend Tree; abrupt changes in the parameter can still produce visual jitter if clips or transitions are not tuned. If needed, smooth the Speed value using Mathf. Lerp or damping to produce natural acceleration. Finally, toggling a layer's weight in script is similar: get the layer index by name and call SetLayerWeight to change the influence of that layer at runtime.

keyIdea.title: Script control
keyIdea.text: Update the Animator's float parameter each frame to drive blends; clamp and optionally smooth the value to match thresholds and avoid jitter.

content.html:
Code Walkthrough
PlayerMovementAnimator pattern
// Update speed from input, clamp, set Animator float
currentSpeed = Mathf.Clamp(currentSpeed, 0f, 5f);
playerAnimator.SetFloat("Speed", currentSpeed);
  • Ensure parameter name matches Animator exactly.
  • Smooth abrupt changes with interpolation to avoid visual jitter.
  • Decide if root motion or a controller moves the transform.
Layer control example
To toggle an UpperBody layer, get the layer index by name and call SetLayerWeight(index, value). Use 1 for full influence and 0 to disable. A short toggle on input allows testing while playing.
Key Takeaway

Scripted parameters and layer weights let you combine runtime control with authored blends for responsive animation.

screens.title: Animation Layers — purpose and blending
screens.subtitle: Run multiple state machines concurrently and mix them by weight

narration.text: Animation Layers allow you to play more than one state machine at the same time inside the Animator. The Base Layer typically contains locomotion and full-body states. Additional layers can define gestures, facial expressions, or upper-body actions. Each layer has a Weight between zero and one, which controls how much of its output contributes to the final animation. Blending mode matters: Override replaces the lower layers for the masked bones, and Additive adds motions on top of them, which is useful for subtle adjustments. A practical example is keeping a Base Layer playing a locomotion Blend Tree while an UpperBody layer plays a wave animation. Set the UpperBody layer's Weight to 1 and use an Avatar Mask to restrict the layer to the spine and arms. Common pitfalls include forgetting to set the layer's Weight to a non-zero value so it never influences the character, or using Override mode with a mask that unintentionally includes legs. Always test by toggling the weight at runtime. The modularity of layers makes animation systems easier to author and debug because you can isolate gesture logic from locomotion.

keyIdea.title: Layer fundamentals
keyIdea.text: Layers run separate state machines; weight and blending mode determine how they combine with lower layers.

content.html:
Definition
Animation Layers

Separate state machines that can play concurrently. Each has a Weight and Blending mode to control influence over final poses.

  • Weight: 0–1 influence value.
  • Blending: Override replaces, Additive adds to lower layers.
  • Use: gestures, facial animations, or upper-body actions independent of base locomotion.
Practical scenario
Create an UpperBody layer, set Weight to 1, set Blending to Override, assign a mask that includes spine and arms, and place a Wave clip in that layer's state machine. Toggle Weight at runtime to control visibility.
Pro Tip

Use Additive for subtle facial or breathing adjustments and Override for full pose replacement on masked bones.

screens.title: Creating an Avatar Mask for the Upper Body
screens.subtitle: Select bones so the layer only affects intended body parts

narration.text: An Avatar Mask acts like a stencil that selects which bones a layer affects. To create one, right-click in the Project window and choose Create → Avatar Mask. In the Inspector open the Humanoid tab and deselect all, then manually toggle the Spine, Chest, UpperChest, Shoulders, Arms, Forearms, and Hands on. Name it UpperBodyMask and assign it to the UpperBody layer's Mask field in the Animator Layers tab. This ensures the UpperBody layer only influences those bones; the legs and hips remain driven by the Base Layer. A frequent mistake is leaving more bones enabled than intended or forgetting to assign the mask, which causes unexpected blending. After assigning the mask, test by playing the Wave animation and observing which bones move. If legs move, re-open the mask and uncheck lower-body bones. Remember that naming conventions in rigs might differ; adjust selections to match your humanoid rig's bone names. The mask gives you precise control and prevents layers from fighting over the same bones. Creating an Avatar Mask for the Upper Body means an avatar mask specifies bone-level inclusion so a layer affects only chosen body parts like spine and arms.. In practical terms, select bones so the layer only affects intended body parts. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Avatar Mask
keyIdea.text: An Avatar Mask specifies bone-level inclusion so a layer affects only chosen body parts like spine and arms.

content.html:
Process Flow
Create UpperBodyMask
  1. Project window → Create → Avatar Mask. Name it UpperBodyMask.
  2. In the Inspector, open Humanoid and deselect all body parts.
  3. Manually enable Spine, Chest, UpperChest, Shoulders, Arms, Forearms, Hands.
  4. Assign the mask to the UpperBody layer in the Animator Layers tab.
  5. Play the Wave animation and verify only upper-body bones move.
Checklist
  • Mask assigned to the correct layer.
  • Layer Weight > 0 when testing.
  • Bone selection matches your rig's naming.
Common Mistake

Including legs in the mask or forgetting to assign it will let the layer override lower-body motion unexpectedly.

screens.title: Combining Blend Trees and Layers
screens.subtitle: A modular setup: Locomotion on Base Layer and gestures on UpperBody layer

narration.text: A powerful pattern is to place locomotion Blend Trees on the Base Layer and put gestures or expressions on separate layers with masks. The Base Layer contains the Locomotion blend driven by Speed, handling root movement or controller-driven movement. The UpperBody layer contains a simple state machine with a Wave or Punch animation and uses an UpperBodyMask so only the torso and arms animate. The layer's Weight controls whether the gesture influences the final pose. In practice, you might set the UpperBody layer to Override and toggle its weight from zero to one when the player triggers an action. This modular architecture reduces coupling: tuning a wave does not require altering locomotion states. When debugging, watch for animation conflicts where both layers attempt the same bones; masks and blending modes are the control points. Also use small transition durations on both layers to avoid snap changes. For facial or breathing tweaks, consider Additive blending layers stacked above Override layers for subtle offsets. Overall, this modular approach scales well: you can add face, upper-body, and item-holding layers independently. Combining Blend Trees and Layers means put locomotion in base layer and independent gestures in separate masked layers to reduce coupling and simplify tuning.. In practical terms, a modular setup: locomotion on base layer and gestures on upperbody layer. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Modular animation
keyIdea.text: Put locomotion in Base Layer and independent gestures in separate masked layers to reduce coupling and simplify tuning.

content.html:
Architecture
Base Layer + UpperBody Layer
  • Base Layer: Locomotion Blend Tree driven by Speed, full-body or root motion.
  • UpperBody Layer: Gesture state machine, Masked to spine and arms, Blending = Override.
  • Control: Layer Weight toggled via script to enable or disable gestures at runtime.
Runtime control
Use GetLayerIndex and SetLayerWeight to toggle the UpperBody layer from script when an input is detected, enabling gestures without stopping locomotion.
Key Takeaway

Modularity makes animation systems scalable: add or tune layers independently of the base locomotion blend.

screens.title: Common pitfalls and fixes
screens.subtitle: Threshold mismatches, unlooped clips, mask errors, and layer weight mistakes

narration.text: When building Blend Trees and Layers a few mistakes occur repeatedly. First, incorrect threshold values cause an animation like Run to never play because the runtime parameter doesn't reach that threshold. Fix this by aligning thresholds with your input scaling or by adjusting input mapping or max speed. Second, animation clips that aren't looped will cause pops during continuous blending; enable Loop Time in the clip's import settings or trim the animation so start and end poses match. Third, Avatar Masks that include unintended bones will let a layer override parts of the body you expected to remain driven by the Base Layer. Reopen the mask and uncheck lower-body bones if legs move unexpectedly. Fourth, forgetting to set a layer's Weight leaves it inactive — remember to initialize weights in code or Inspector when testing. Finally, abrupt parameter changes can produce visual jitter; smooth parameter updates with interpolation if needed. For each issue, test in the Animator preview and in the Game view while toggling the relevant inputs; these quick checks help isolate whether the problem is an authored asset, mask selection, or runtime control.

keyIdea.title: Troubleshooting
keyIdea.text: Check thresholds, loop settings, mask bones, and layer weights; smooth parameter updates to avoid jitter.

content.html:
Common Mistakes
Troubleshooting checklist
  • Threshold mismatch: Lower or raise thresholds to match actual runtime ranges.
  • Unlooped clips: Enable Loop Time for continuous locomotion clips.
  • Mask errors: Verify Avatar Mask bone toggles to exclude legs if needed.
  • Layer weight: Ensure the layer weight is set above zero when you expect it to act.
  • Parameter jitter: Smooth values with interpolation to avoid abrupt visual changes.
Quick fixes
Use Animator preview, small transition durations, and runtime toggles to isolate the root cause of visual artifacts.

screens.title: Lab: Implement the 1D Blend Tree and UpperBody Layer
screens.subtitle: Step sequence to complete the hands-on activity in the chapter

narration.text: This lab guides you through the hands-on activity: implement a 1D Blend Tree for locomotion and an UpperBody layer with an Avatar Mask for waving. Step one: import a humanoid model with Idle, Walk, Run, and Wave clips and ensure the Rig is Humanoid. Step two: create an Animator Controller, set Idle as the default state, and create a Locomotion Blend Tree set to 1D with the Speed parameter. Add motion fields with thresholds 0, 2, and 5 for Idle, Walk, and Run. Step three: add transitions between Idle and Locomotion based on Speed conditions and set Transition Duration to 0.2 with Has Exit Time unchecked. Step four: create a new layer named UpperBody, set Weight to 1 and Blending to Override. Create an Avatar Mask called UpperBodyMask that includes the spine and arms only, assign it to the layer, and place Wave as the default state in that layer. Step five: attach the CharacterAnimatorController script to your character, ensure animator references are assigned, and run the scene. Use WASD to vary Speed and Space to toggle the UpperBody layer weight. Observe that legs continue locomotion while the arms wave — that's the designed behavior to confirm.

keyIdea.text: Import clips, create 1D Blend Tree for Speed, add UpperBody layer with Avatar Mask, and control layer weight by script.

  2. Create Animator Controller and assign to character.
  3. Drag Idle into Animator as default state.

  1. Create Locomotion Blend Tree (1D). Add Speed parameter.
  2. Add Idle(0), Walk(2), Run(5). Preview and adjust thresholds.

  1. Add new layer named UpperBody, set Weight to 1 and Blending to Override.
  2. Create UpperBodyMask and include spine, chest, arms, hands.

  1. Attach CharacterAnimatorController, verify Animator reference.
  2. Run scene. Use movement keys to change Speed. Press Space to toggle the wave layer weight.
Key Takeaway

Follow the steps and verify in both the Animator preview and Game view to ensure blends and mask boundaries behave as expected.

screens.title: Assessment scenarios and thought questions
screens.subtitle: Diagnose issues and choose the right Mecanim features

narration.text: To consolidate learning, practice diagnosing three assessment scenarios. Scenario one: you need locomotion blended by speed and an independent punch animation that should not affect the legs. The correct approach is a 1D Blend Tree for locomotion on the Base Layer and a separate Animation Layer with an Avatar Mask limited to the right arm for the punch. Scenario two: walking animations occasionally pop inside a blend even though Speed is updated. The likely problem is mismatched loop points in your animation clip rather than the Blend Tree thresholds, so inspect the clip's start and end poses and enable Loop Time if appropriate. Scenario three: a gesture layer isn't visible during play. Check that the layer's Weight is set above zero and that the Avatar Mask doesn't exclude the intended bones. As you practice, ask yourself: does this problem originate from authored assets, mask configuration, or runtime parameter control? Framing issues this way makes troubleshooting faster. Try these scenarios hands-on and explain your fix out loud to reinforce the decision process. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Key Concepts — What to Remember
screens.subtitle: Three compact reminders to carry forward

narration.text: Remember three practical concepts. First, Blend Trees consolidate multiple motion clips into a single state driven by parameters, and they are essential for smooth locomotion between Idle, Walk, and Run. Second, Animation Layers let you run separate state machines concurrently; layer weight and blending mode define how much they affect the final pose. Third, Avatar Masks give you bone-level control so a layer influences only selected body parts, enabling gestures like waving or punching without disrupting lower-body locomotion. Keep in mind common pitfalls: thresholds must match runtime ranges, clips must loop cleanly, and masks must be carefully configured. These three building blocks—Blend Trees, Layers, and Avatar Masks—are the practical tools you'll use to compose responsive and modular character animation systems. keyIdea.text: Threshold alignment, blending mode choice, and mask validation are the fastest ways to avoid common animation errors.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.2 › Quick Reference
Align thresholds
Ensure parameter ranges match your thresholds so each clip plays when expected during tests.
Choose blending mode
Override for replacing masked bones, Additive for subtle additive offsets like facial tweaks.
Validate masks
Confirm the Avatar Mask selects only intended bones; fix any accidental inclusions.
When you test, toggle layer weights and scrub Blend Tree parameters in the Animator preview to quickly surface configuration problems.
